### Related literature {#sec-literature}

The real-options foundation rests on @mcdonald1986value for optimal timing of irreversible investment and @pindyck1988irreversible for capacity choice. @guo2005investment model demand with regime-dependent drift and volatility, and @decamps2006irreversible study the choice between two irreversible projects of different scale. None of these includes strategic interaction, training-inference allocation, or default risk; here the scale choice is in that tradition, while the $L \to H$ transition is an exogenous Poisson regime switch. In operations management the closest construct is resource flexibility [@vanmieghem2003capacity]: @chod2005resource show that a flexible resource allocated across products *after* demand is observed substitutes for capacity. Compute is flexible in that sense, but the allocation here is a commitment made at installation whose training component pays off only in a different demand regime, and it is priced jointly with the firm's default decision.

Strategic real-options models replace the single decision maker with rivals whose entry erodes the option value of waiting [@grenadier2002option]. The closest is @huisman2015strategic, who study a duopoly with joint timing and capacity choice; I add endogenous default risk, training-inference allocation, and regime switching. @aguerrevere2003equilibrium and @aguerrevere2009real link installed capacity and competitive intensity to the composition of firm value between assets in place and growth options, an antecedent of the training-beta conjecture of @sec-discussion. @lambrecht2003real study duopoly real options under incomplete information, related to the mistaken beliefs about the arrival rate $\lambda$ here but without the allocation or default mechanisms.

The paper also connects to patent races and R&D competition. @loury1979market and @reinganum1982strategic model firms choosing R&D intensity to accelerate a stochastic Poisson breakthrough, and @harris1987racing derive a discouragement effect for lagging firms; the follower here also enters late, though following is the better role. @weeds2002strategic places a winner-take-all patent race in a real-options duopoly and shows that competition can delay rather than hasten investment; the entry game here has a related feature, a second-mover advantage at the date of first investment. The key departure is the dual role of capacity: inference earns revenue before the switch and training determines position after it.

The firm's default decision follows the structural credit-risk tradition of @merton1974pricing and @leland1994corporate, a literature that already embeds regime switching: @hackbarth2006capital let cash flows depend on a two-state macroeconomic regime, and @chen2010macroeconomic and @bhamra2010levered add a consumption-based pricing kernel. The boundary of Proposition 2 is therefore not the first derived in a regime-switching environment; those papers solve the fully coupled system with regime-contingent boundaries, whereas @eq-default-boundary uses a single boundary that embeds the switch in unconditional expectation. The Leland framework suits public-debt issuers; for the VC-backed archetypes in the calibration, "default" should be read broadly as financial distress (failed funding round, liquidity crisis), consistent with @gornall2020squaring. The investment-financing framework follows @hackbarth2012corporate.

The model's technology assumptions come from the economics of AI: training exhibits power-law scaling [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training], and @agrawal2019economics frame AI as a prediction technology connecting inference demand to value creation. @aghion2019artificial, @acemoglu2024simple, @korinek2024scenarios, and @jones2024agi analyze the growth implications of transformative AI in general equilibrium; the present paper is partial equilibrium and complements them with a firm-level investment and allocation problem. On the allocation margin, the closest analog is @akcigit2018growth on exploitation versus exploration R&D.

The marginal contribution is a set of results the closest models do not generate. In the papers that combine irreversible investment with endogenous default [@mauer2005real; @hackbarth2014capital; @sundaresan2015dynamic; @kumar2018optimal], installed capital is homogeneous, and the regime-switching credit models take the size of the growth option as exogenous, so the firm has no decision that trades current revenue against the value of surviving to a later regime. The training fraction $\phi$ is that decision here: it governs how the default boundary responds to beliefs, and it carries most of the expected-value cost of a mistaken belief. The allocation problems closest in structure [@akcigit2018growth; @chod2005resource] are solved for firms whose survival is not at stake. On timing, the strategic real-options models above obtain early investment from a race to be first, whereas here competition brings investment forward of the switch although following is the better role at the date of first investment.
